title: How we know
lede: What Lake Watch is built from, how it decides each lake's status, how it compares with optical images, and where it falls short.
can: NISAR made {cloud_looks} valid looks across {cloud_lakes} of {lake_count} lakes between {cloud_start} and {cloud_end}, the weeks when SUPARCO's updates reported cloud limiting optical imagery.

Each lake gets one plain level, No change, Watch, Alert: growing or Decrease noted, from its own earlier passes on each viewing track, with the noise it was judged against shown beside it and a short message that says what to do.
Passes that look wrong for their track (too bright, too dark, or outliers) are left out and listed with their reason, never read as growth or shrinkage.
cannot: Map a lake's exact shoreline. Against Sentinel-2, radar water {optical_overlap}, one date per lake.
See a lake draw down onto wet sediment (the radar sees about a tenth to a fifth of such a decrease), frozen lakes, lakes under 0.05 km² or wind-roughened water reliably.

Say when or whether a lake will burst. An Alert is slow-growth monitoring, 5–12 days after a change begins, not outburst warning, and Lake Watch is indicative screening on provisional data, not an official warning service.

sections.title: Lake method
paragraphs: Lake Watch reads NISAR GCOV passes, HH and HV, from {cloud_start} on: NASA's provisional release (P05023) for passes up to 21 Oct 2026 and NASA's standard GCOV product (P05036) for later ones; this build uses {processing_versions}. Calibrated passes only, and one viewing track is never mixed with another. The cloud window for the headline count is {cloud_start} to {cloud_end}, while SUPARCO's 2 Jul and 5 Aug updates reported cloud limiting optical imagery. SUPARCO's 2 Jul update rests on one 16 Jun image; its 5 Aug update used images from 6 Jul to 5 Aug and reports 105 lakes unfrozen, up from 40 (space4climate.gov.pk, GLOF monitoring status 5 August 2026).

Water rule (method {method_id}). Each pass is first smoothed with a {lee_box} by {lee_box} pixel Lee filter on linear power, which calms speckle and keeps a lake's edge. A pixel is water when its HH is at least {drop_db} dB below the median HH of the 6 km search window in that pass. HV is not used for water: lake HV sits close to the radar's noise floor, as does the dry ground around it, and asking for both made small lakes read 40–90% low. HV still screens passes.

Shadow and layover. Inside the lake zone nothing is masked: a flat lake surface is almost never in radar shadow or layover, which fall on the valley walls. The walls are left out of the window median that water is measured against, mapped from the Copernicus GLO-30 terrain model with the viewing direction fitted to each track (looking about 255° from north on ascending passes and 105° on descending ones, at 40° incidence). The earlier two-view rule, which removed a pixel dark from only one side as shadow, removed 15–42% of the real water at the four lakes checked against Sentinel-2, and is no longer used.

Against Sentinel-2 at Attabad, Passu, Karambar and Shazore (38 radar and optical pairs from summer 2026), this rule overlaps optical water with a median IoU of 0.57–0.69, against 0.10–0.62 for the old one, and reads areas within −16% to +20% of optical (the old one −11% to −88%).

Each area is the water inside the lake's outline, buffered by 200 m, where it has one (from OpenStreetMap), and otherwise inside a search circle around its coordinates, 1 km unless the lake sets a smaller one for a small pond. A lake larger than its zone or its 6 km radar window is only partly counted, and wet shore and exposed sediment flats inside the zone read as water. The data file's own note reads: "{notes}"
list: A pass whose window brightness is far from its own track's median is left out, listed on the lake with its reason, and never read as growth or shrinkage.

A pass is also left out when the share of dark pixels in its window, or its window-median HV, is an outlier among its own track's passes (robust z-score above {outlier_z}). The 5 Sep 2026 pass on track 156A, anomalous over the Hunza lakes, is left out by hand wherever this test does not already catch it; each lake lists the reason.
A pass is compared once its track has at least {min_looks} earlier valid passes. Until one has, the status is Not enough NISAR looks yet.
At least {min_observable_pct}% of the lake zone ({min_observable}) must be observable, not missing or masked. Otherwise the status is Not observable, and no area is shown.

Every valid pass, on any track, is compared with the median of up to {baseline_passes} earlier valid passes on its own track: z = (area − baseline) / noise. The noise is the spread of that track's pass-to-pass differences over up to {noise_passes} passes, never below {noise_floor_km2} km² or {noise_rel_floor_pct}% of the baseline.

Levels. Alert: growing when two valid passes in a row, on any tracks, have z of +{change_factor} or more. Watch when one pass has z beyond ±{change_factor}, or when the running sum of the z values (a CUSUM with k = {cusum_k}) reaches {cusum_h}. Decrease noted when two passes in a row have z of −{change_factor} or less: information only, never an Alert, because the radar sees a drawdown onto wet sediment at only about a tenth to a fifth of its size. Otherwise No change. A level holds until evidence clears it: Alert: growing until two valid passes in a row have z under +{change_factor}; Watch until a valid pass is within ±{change_factor} with the CUSUM under 4; Decrease noted until two valid passes in a row have z above −{change_factor}. A higher level replaces a lower one; the level's date stays the date that set it, and the message gives the newest pass's z. A frozen spell suspends any level, and after it the first two passes per track rebuild the baseline. A newer pass that could not be read never hides a level; the status says which pass and why.

Version rule. A track's first pass on a NISAR processing version that its baseline lacks can raise a Watch but cannot be one of the two passes of an Alert; a second pass on that version enters the baseline. When every track's latest pass is its first on a new version, Alerts pause for about two to three weeks and the status says "Alerts paused"; otherwise it names the one track whose pass cannot count toward an Alert, since the other tracks still can.
Passes taken while a lake was frozen are not compared at all, and the first {after_open_passes} passes per track after it opens only rebuild the baseline: they set no level.
Not measurable. A lake whose Sentinel-2 check overlaps radar water with an IoU under {min_validation_iou} gets no level; its area is shown as information only, and the lake says why.

Not yet validated against Sentinel-2. A lake gets a level only with a current Sentinel-2 check: one made for this water method, this zone and this lake point. A lake with none yet, with one made for an older method, zone or point, or whose check found no usable pair or failed, gets no level and says why; each refresh checks it again, and reuses the checks that are current. A newly accepted lake is checked in the same run against the summer archive (every pass since 17 Jun 2026 is fetched). It stays Not yet validated only when it has no valid NISAR pass between 15 Jun and 30 Sep, or no Sentinel-2 scene within ±3 days of one with at most 20% cloud over the window and at least 80% of the lake zone clear.

Every Watch, Alert and Decrease noted carries a short message written from these numbers: what changed and by how much against its baseline, over which passes and dates, how sure (the z values, one pass or two), what it is not (not an outburst forecast; drawdown is hard to see; it comes 5–12 days after the change began), and what to do: check recent optical imagery or the site, and contact GBDMA or PDMA. Official warnings come from PMD, NDMA, GBDMA and PDMA.
Each pass is compared only with earlier passes from its own track. Read the numbers and their noise, not only the level.

sections.title: Sentinel-2 cross-check and what is not validated
paragraphs: Where a clear Sentinel-2 scene was close in time, we compared one NISAR pass with it inside each lake's zone (its outline where it has one, otherwise its search circle). Sites with no lake now are not compared. Only pairs in the open-water season are used, the clearest one per lake, because a frozen or snow-covered lake has no open water for optical to see; each row names the season. The rows below are copied from the data file.
afterTable: Radar water {optical_overlap}. Radar counts wet shore inside the zone and is limited by speckle at small lakes, and optical water misses shaded or very dark lakes, so neither is a clean reference.
This zone comparison is not a validation of lake extent. It compares two rough water maps of the same zone, on one date each.
The SUPARCO area comparison was skipped because no SUPARCO lake IDs or locations have been supplied.
Not validated: frozen lakes, lakes under 0.05 km², and wind-roughened water.

sections.title: Frozen lakes
paragraphs: L-band radar does not see a mountain lake freeze. New ice under dry snow stays as dark as open water, while frozen ground around the lake darkens and reads as more water: at Shazore the radar area rose by 44% after freeze-up, although Sentinel-2 showed the lake under snow and ice from 19 Oct 2026. So Lake Watch decides whether a lake is probably frozen from air temperature, and from Sentinel-2 when a clear image shows it, never from the radar area.

Frozen (likely): the NASA POWER daily mean air temperature, moved from its grid cell's height to the lake's height (from the Copernicus DEM) at {lapse_c_per_km} °C per km, has been below 0 °C on at least {freeze_cold_run_days} days in a row, with at least {freeze_fdd} freezing degree-days since 1 Sep. Frozen (seen by Sentinel-2): snow or ice covers at least {s2_frozen_pct}% of the lake itself (its outline without the buffer, or for a lake without an outline its summer radar water core, counting only the pixels seen clear) in the clearest Sentinel-2 image of the last {s2_freeze_days} days that sees at least {s2_freeze_clear_pct}% of the lake zone and half of the lake itself clear of cloud, cloud shadow and their 100 m edge. Water on at least {s2_open_pct}% of the lake itself in such an image means open water seen by Sentinel-2. Either reading holds until other evidence: a snow-covered lake stays frozen until a clear image shows open water or the break-up rules release it, and a lake seen open stays so until a new run of {freeze_cold_run_days} days below 0 °C.

Break-up likely: a frozen lake has had at least {breakup_warm_run_days} days in a row above 0 °C, or a radar pass shows its core at least {breakup_contrast_db} dB brighter against its surroundings than in summer, in both HH and HV, with a dark share at least {breakup_dark_drop} lower: a brightening that matches ice going out, as Shazore's lake core showed in late June 2026. The lake is released after {thaw_warm_run_days} warm days in a row and one radar pass back within its summer range ("Radar back within its summer range"), or by a clear Sentinel-2 image of open water ("Open water seen by Sentinel-2"). A lake with no radar summer level to check against is released by the warm days alone, and then says "No freeze signal in air temperature since" that date, with open water not confirmed by radar or Sentinel-2.

While a lake is frozen or its ice is breaking up, it gets no level (no Watch, Alert or other); this comes before every other status except No lake now. Its area is still shown, greyed, as not an open-water measurement, its radar water layer is hidden, and passes taken while it was frozen are greyed in the chart and the table and left out of the comparison, the noise and the summer level. Freeze-up is called only from 1 Sep to 31 May, but a frozen lake stays frozen after 31 May until the break-up and release rules release it, since a high lake's ice can go out in late June or July; freezing degree-days start again each 1 Sep. When the newest air temperature is more than {power_stale_days} days old, or cannot be fetched, the last check stands and says since when it has not been refreshed; a lake never checked is not assessed and keeps the usual status.
list: Winter radar is untested. The radar data so far end in early November, just after freeze-up; whether these lakes brighten on radar in mid-winter is not known, and new ice under dry snow can read as dark as open water, so a radar pass "back within its summer range" in late winter or early spring may not mean the ice has gone. The rule will be tested again with late-January data, these two points included.

Without a clear Sentinel-2 image the rule can be one to two weeks late: in July 2026 it released Shazore on 19 July, about two weeks after Sentinel-2 showed the lake partly open on 6 July. At freeze-up it was on time there: the air met the rule on 18 October 2026, between a Sentinel-2 view of open water on 9 October and one of snow and ice on 19 October.

The air temperature is an estimate, not a measurement at the lake: a reanalysis value for a cell about 50 km across, moved to the lake's height with one lapse rate, while Karakoram valley lapse rates vary between about 4 and 8 °C per km.
Frozen describes the lake surface from air temperature or an optical image. The radar does not show the ice, and Lake Watch says nothing about how thick it is.
Air temperature alone never shows open water; only a clear Sentinel-2 image can.

sections.title: The data
paragraphs: Lake Watch is built from public sources. Only the first two are satellite images.

head: Source
What we used it for
Status
rows: NISAR L2 GCOV, provisional and standard (NASA, from the ASF archive)
Every lake area and radar picture: HH and HV, every calibrated pass over each lake from 17 June 2026, {processing_versions}, read as a 6 km window per pass.

Passes up to 21 Oct 2026 are the provisional release (P05023): not validated, and NASA expects to reprocess it, so values may move. Later passes are NASA's standard GCOV product (P05036); we have seen no validation statement for it. A lake whose track spans both says so, because a calibration change can shift areas.
The optical cross-check: MNDWI water on a clear scene close in date to one NISAR pass.
Optical, so it fails under cloud; a rough reference, not ground truth.
The cloud window and the context: optical updates of 2 July and 5 August 2026.

The freeze check: daily mean and minimum air temperature at each lake from 1 Sep, moved to the lake's height.
A reanalysis estimate for a cell about 50 km across, not a measurement at the lake; it arrives a few days late.
Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (ESA and Airbus, via Earth Search)
The height of each lake's surface, measured once, so the air temperature can be moved from its grid cell to the lake.
About ±100 m where the lake has no flat water surface in the DEM.
Where each lake's search zone sits.
From published inventories, papers, OpenStreetMap and Sentinel-2 imagery, each named on its lake card. A location check against 2026 imagery removed points that were not lakes.

sections.title: Limits
list: A lake drawing down onto wet sediment is nearly invisible to the radar: wet, smooth flats are as dark as water, so it sees about a tenth to a fifth of such a decrease (Attabad lost about 1 km² of Sentinel-2 water between August and October 2026; its radar area hardly moved).
An Alert comes 5–12 days after a change begins in Hunza, where three tracks pass, and 8–12 days in Chitral, where two do.
This is slow-growth monitoring, not outburst warning: an outburst takes hours.

False-alarm and miss rates are modelled from one season's pass-to-pass noise, not observed: no lake grew in the 2026 data, so no miss has been seen. With so few differences per lake the noise itself is uncertain by about ±40%. They will be estimated again after one more season.
Lakes below about 0.05 km² are limited by speckle: there the noise floor of {noise_floor_km2} km² is a large share of the lake.

Replayed on the 2026 series, the levels raised no growth Alert. Attabad's September drawdown shows as Watches around 10 Sep, not as a Decrease noted: with the noise floored at 2% of its 4.3–4.7 km² baseline, its 063D pass of 10 Sep is z = −1.4. The method study's own replay, which had no 2% floor, called a Decrease noted there; the floor binds only at Attabad and does not change how soon its growth would be seen (25%, about 1.1 km²).
Areas are water inside a search zone, so a lake larger than its zone is only partly counted, and wet shore inside it reads as water.
Radar pictures are NISAR GCOV crops on the UTM grid, north up; they are pictures, not interactive map overlays.
A level compares a lake only with its own earlier passes, each against its own track; it is not an absolute size.
Passes up to 21 Oct 2026 are provisional NISAR data, subject to reprocessing; later passes are NASA's standard product, and a track that spans both can shift with the calibration change.

sections.title: Check it yourself
paragraphs: docs/DATA_SOURCES.md lists every source and its licence status. The pipeline in processing/ rebuilds every number on this page: lakes-search, lakes-fetch, lakes-build, lakes-check and lakes-freeze.
Not an official warning service. For warnings, use the Pakistan Meteorological Department, NDMA, GBDMA and PDMA.
